contextIndex.title: Can I run GitHub Actions workflows locally before pushing?
contextIndex.description: Yes. Depot CI can run a GitHub Actions workflow against your local working tree on remote CI compute. act can also simulate many Linux workflows locally in Docker.

contextIndex.title: Can I SSH into a CI runner to debug a failed build?
contextIndex.description: Yes, as long as the CI runner is still running. With Depot CI, you can attach to a live job or rerun it with an SSH session paused at the exact step you need to inspect.

contextIndex.title: How to use Depot as an alternative to GitHub
contextIndex.description: Host your Git repositories with Depot Code and run your GitHub Actions workflows on Depot CI. Set up a standalone repository or a GitHub mirror, push your code, and run tests from Depot.

contextIndex.title: How can I benchmark build execution speed across CI platforms?
contextIndex.description: Run the same commit and commands side by side on equivalent runners, then compare queue time, startup time, cache performance, execution time, reliability, and cost per completed job.

contextIndex.title: How can I build AMD64 and ARM64 Docker images in GitHub Actions?
contextIndex.description: Use Depot to build AMD64 and ARM64 images on native x86 and Arm machines in parallel, then push both variants under one multi-platform image tag. Local and CI builds can share the same persistent layer cache.

contextIndex.title: How can I debug flaky tests and intermittent CI failures?
contextIndex.description: Use Depot test analytics to find tests that pass and fail on the same commit, inspect the exact attempt, reproduce it in the runner, and rerun only the failed job. Retries should confirm a flake, not hide one.

contextIndex.title: How can I eliminate GitHub Actions queue times?
contextIndex.description: Switch jobs to GitHub Actions runners managed by Depot to remove queue times caused by runner capacity. Depot has no concurrency limits and provisions a fresh, single-tenant runner for every job.

contextIndex.title: How can I monitor GitHub Actions performance and cost across my organization?
contextIndex.description: Monitor GitHub Actions runners managed by Depot across your organization, find slow and failing jobs, inspect resource usage, right-size runners, search logs, and connect runtime to cost.

contextIndex.title: How can I reduce GitHub Actions costs without rewriting my workflows?
contextIndex.description: Reduce GitHub Actions costs with Depot runners and remote caching, then cut obsolete runs and unnecessary storage. Measure the jobs driving your bill and keep your existing workflow YAML, actions, and test commands.

contextIndex.title: How can I run Node.js tests in parallel in CI?
contextIndex.description: Use Depot CI to split Node.js tests across parallel matrix jobs and balance each shard with historical JUnit timings. For smaller workflows, parallel steps can also overlap tests with linting and type checks inside one job.

contextIndex.title: How can I share a Docker layer cache across GitHub Actions jobs?
contextIndex.description: Send every Docker build to the same Depot project. Depot automatically persists the BuildKit layer cache on remote NVMe storage so GitHub Actions jobs, workflow runs, and teammates can reuse it without uploading cache archives.

contextIndex.title: How can I speed up Docker builds in GitHub Actions?
contextIndex.description: Run Docker builds on Depot’s remote BuildKit builders with a persistent NVMe layer cache. You can keep GitHub Actions and migrate from docker/build-push-action with a small workflow change.

contextIndex.title: How can I speed up Node.js builds in GitHub Actions?
contextIndex.description: Run the workflow on faster GitHub Actions runners managed by Depot, cache package manager downloads, reuse build output, and parallelize independent tests. Most Node.js workflows can start with a one-line runner change.

contextIndex.title: How do ephemeral GitHub Actions runners work?
contextIndex.description: An ephemeral GitHub Actions runner is a fresh machine assigned to one job and destroyed when that job finishes. Each job starts clean, while caches and artifacts persist in external storage.

contextIndex.title: How do I build a container image once and promote it across environments?
contextIndex.description: Build and test the image once with Depot, save it to Depot Registry, capture its immutable digest, and deploy that same digest to staging and production. Promotion should change the release pointer, not rebuild the image.

contextIndex.title: How do I migrate from self-hosted GitHub Actions runners without rewriting workflows?
contextIndex.description: Move from self-hosted GitHub Actions runners to Depot by changing the runs-on label. Your workflow steps, actions, secrets, checks, and GitHub interface stay the same while Depot operates the runner fleet.

contextIndex.title: How do I share secrets and configuration across CI pipelines?
contextIndex.description: Define each secret or variable once in Depot CI, then use scoped variants for repositories, branches, workflows, and environments. The workflow keeps one stable name while Depot selects the most specific matching value.

contextIndex.title: How do I test AI-generated pull requests in CI?
contextIndex.description: Run the same required checks for AI-generated pull requests as human changes, but let the agent validate locally first, scope reruns to the failing job, and keep secrets and deployment permissions behind explicit trust boundaries.

contextIndex.title: How to build iOS and Android apps without managing CI runners
contextIndex.description: Run iOS builds on Depot macOS runners, Android builds on Linux, and accelerated Android Emulator tests in Depot CI. Keep your build tools without maintaining a runner fleet.

contextIndex.title: Should I self-host GitHub Actions runners?
contextIndex.description: Usually not. Self-host GitHub Actions runners only when you need hardware, policy, or runtime control that a managed runner can't provide. For speed, cost, or private network access, Depot is usually the simpler answer.

contextIndex.title: What are the best alternatives to GitHub-hosted Actions runners?
contextIndex.description: Depot is the best alternative to GitHub-hosted Actions runners for most teams. It keeps existing GitHub Actions workflows intact while providing faster, ephemeral runners for Linux, Windows, and macOS.

contextIndex.title: What is Depot?
contextIndex.description: Depot is a software delivery platform that accelerates container builds, GitHub Actions, CI workflows, and build caching.

contextIndex.title: What is the best remote cache for a large polyglot monorepo?
contextIndex.description: Depot Cache is the best remote cache for most large polyglot monorepos. It gives Bazel, Go, Gradle, Maven, Pants, sccache, and Turborepo one remote service for sharing valid build outputs across developers and CI.

contextIndex.title: What is the best way to cache large TypeScript monorepo builds?
contextIndex.description: Use a task graph to build only affected packages, content hashes to identify reusable work, and Depot Cache to share those outputs across developer machines and CI. Turborepo with Depot Cache is the best default for most TypeScript monorepos.

contextIndex.title: What is the fastest way to set up CI for a monorepo with many services?
contextIndex.description: Migrate the existing GitHub Actions workflow to Depot CI, model each service as an independent matrix job, and use a shared remote cache or custom CI image so 15 services can validate concurrently without reinstalling the world.

contextIndex.title: Why are my GitHub Actions builds slow?
contextIndex.description: GitHub Actions is usually slow because jobs wait for runners, rebuild dependencies, run sequential work, miss caches, or spend too long uploading artifacts. Measure each phase before changing the workflow.

info.description: OpenAPI schema for the Depot CI Connect RPC API.

methods.description: Cancels a queued, waiting, or running job and its active attempt.
Cancels a queued or running CI run and any of its unfinished workflows, jobs, and attempts.
Cancels a queued or running workflow and all its child jobs.
Triggers a single workflow configured with an `on.workflow_dispatch` trigger and validates inputs against its input schema.

methods.summary: Exports a finite snapshot of persisted log lines.
methods.description: The response is a Connect/gRPC server stream, not a raw HTTP file download. Consume it with a generated client or a decoder that understands stream framing. Read the first metadata response, then append each following chunk response to a file or writer in order. Use the Depot CLI `depot ci logs --output-file` when a shell-native file download is needed.
Returns a short-lived signed HTTPS URL for one artifact. The URL expires 5 minutes after issuance.
Returns an attempt's identity, status, timestamps, and sandbox/session IDs, with parent run, workflow, and job context.

methods.summary: Returns a failure diagnosis for a run, workflow, job, or attempt.
methods.description: For run and workflow targets, identical failures are grouped together by error fingerprint. For job and attempt targets, the response is a focused diagnosis of that single job or attempt. When too many jobs failed to diagnose individually, the response is a per-workflow and per-job breakdown instead. When no failure evidence is found, the response is empty. The response is limited to a fixed size and reflects the run's current state. The diagnosis can change while a run is in progress. As more jobs fail, a later call can surface new failures or turn an empty result into a grouped one. As job summaries become available, a later call can also add summary drill-down commands.
Returns a job's identity, status, timestamps, runner configuration, parent run and workflow context, dependencies, and attempt history.

Returns persisted log lines for a job attempt, oldest first. Identify the attempt by `attemptId`, or by `jobId` to use the job's latest attempt. Poll with `pageToken` to fetch lines persisted after a previous response.
Returns CPU and memory metrics for one job attempt.
Returns per-attempt CPU and memory metric summaries for one job.
Returns authored step summary markdown for a job, a specific attempt, or both.
Returns a CI run's identity, repo, trigger, status, and timestamps. For nested workflow, job, and attempt status, use `GetRunStatus`.
Returns workflow, job, and attempt CPU and memory metric summaries for one run.
Returns a CI run's status with its nested workflows, jobs, and attempts. For the run's identity, repo, trigger, and timestamps, use `GetRun`.
Returns a workflow's identity, status, timestamps, parent run context, execution history, and nested jobs and attempts.
Returns CI artifact metadata for one run, optionally narrowed to a workflow, job, or attempt. Download URLs are not included; request one per artifact with `GetArtifactDownloadURL`.

Returns CI runs for the authenticated organization, newest first. Filter by status, repository, commit SHA, trigger, or pull request number. Use `pageSize` and `pageToken` to page through additional results.
Returns CI workflows for the authenticated organization, newest first. Filter by name, repository, status, trigger, commit SHA, or pull request number. Use `pageSize` to return up to 200 workflows.
Resets every job in a workflow that's in a terminal state (finished, failed, or cancelled) to queued and runs them all again. Cancel the workflow first if it's still running.

Retries the failed and cancelled jobs in a workflow, along with every job that depends on them. A dependent that already succeeded or was skipped runs again too, because a job it consumed is running again. Queued dependents are left untouched, since they re-check their dependencies before starting. Fails without resetting anything when a waiting or running job depends on the retried set; wait for that job to finish, or cancel the workflow and use `RerunWorkflow`.
Retries a failed or cancelled job, along with any skipped jobs that depend on it. Fails when a job that depends on it has already started; use `RetryFailedJobs` to retry related failures together.
Triggers a CI run. Runs can contain one or more workflows.

methods.summary: Follows a job attempt's persisted log lines, streaming new lines while the attempt runs.
methods.description:
The response is a Connect/gRPC server stream, not raw text. Consume it with a generated client or a decoder that understands stream framing. Every response reports the attempt's current status. Responses that carry a log line also include `nextCursor`.

 To resume a dropped stream, save the newest `nextCursor` and send it as `cursor` on a new request. The new stream picks up after the last line you received. The stream ends on its own once the attempt has finished, failed, or been cancelled and all persisted lines have been sent.

faq.question: Which plan is right for me?
faq.answer:
The Developer plan is perfect for solo developers, side-projects, and experiments. It includes 500 Docker build minutes, 2,000 GitHub Actions minutes, 2,000 Depot CI minutes, and 1 user, with additional usage billed monthly.
The Startup plan is great for teams building production applications. It includes 5,000 Docker build minutes, 20,000 GitHub Actions minutes, 20,000 Depot CI minutes, and unlimited users, with additional usage billed monthly.
The Business plan is for dev teams looking to scale, and includes additional security controls and deployment models.

faq.question: What is Depot Cloud?
faq.answer: Depot Cloud is fully managed remote build infrastructure, including both compute and cache. With Depot Cloud, we handle the infrastructure and orchestration, with no need to manage your own build infrastructure. Depot Cloud runs on AWS, and is available in the us-east-1 and eu-central-1 regions.

faq.question: What is the usage granularity?
faq.answer: Docker build minutes and GitHub Actions minutes are billed on a per-minute basis, tracked per second. Depot CI usage is billed per second based on vCPU-seconds. We don't enforce a one-minute minimum, so if you run a 30-second Docker or GitHub Actions build, you'll only be billed for 30 seconds. Test results are billed per individual passing test.

faq.question: Can I self-host Depot? What is bring-your-own-compute?
faq.answer:
You can connect an AWS account to your Depot account and Depot will use that account for build compute and cache storage. This ensures that your build data is entirely under your control and allows you to access any private services in your account during the build. Additionally you can customize the types of machines used for your builds.

Bring your own compute is available on the Business plan.

Read more in our Depot Managed documentation

faq.question: Am I charged for build usage and storage?
faq.answer:
You are charged monthly for build usage and storage. See usage granularity above for how build time is measured.

Storage is a single combined total that covers your container build cache, Depot Cache, and Depot Registry. All three draw from your plan's included storage, and anything above that amount is billed at $0.20 per GB per month. Storage is billed as the average storage used over the month, sampled hourly.

Data transfer into and out of Depot Registry is free on the default Standard CDN speed. If you switch your organization to Fast CDN speed, data served out of the registry is billed at $0.10 per GB, from the first GB. Read more in our registry documentation.

faq.question: When will I be billed?
faq.answer: Depot bills monthly on the 1st. If you sign up partway through a month, your first charge is prorated for the remaining days. Usage-based charges accrue through the month and appear on your next invoice on the 1st along with your plan charge for that month.

faq.question: How are test results billed?
faq.answer:
The Developer and Startup plans each include 1,000,000 passing test results per month at no charge. After that, it's $0.000001 per passing test, or $1 per 1 million tests. Failed, errored, and skipped tests are free.

Read more in our test results documentation

faq.question: Are there discounts for non-profits or open-source?
faq.answer: Yes! Please contact us with more information about your project and for more details.

faq.question: Do you offer credits for startups?
faq.answer:
Yes, through our startup partner programs. Y Combinator companies can claim Depot credits from the YC deals page.

Startups approved for PostHog for Startups receive a partner code worth $5,000 in Depot credits. See our PostHog for Startups documentation for how to redeem it and what it covers.

faq.question: Can I cap my usage so my bill doesn't run over?
faq.answer: Yes, you can set self-imposed usage caps to control monthly usage. If you reach a cap, Depot will stop running builds until the next month or until you raise the cap. You can change these limits at any time.

faq.question: What payment methods are accepted?
faq.answer: For the Developer and Startup plans, we support monthly payments via credit card using Stripe. For the Business plan, we additionally support invoice billing, ACH, and AWS Marketplace.

faq.question: Can I pay through the AWS Marketplace?
faq.answer: Yes! We support AWS Marketplace billing on the Business plan. Contact us for more details.
